[PATH:literature] Wilkinson, R. & Pickett, K. (2009). The Spirit Level: Why Greater Equality Makes Societies Stronger. New York: Bloomsbury Press. — This seminal work provides cross-national empirical evidence linking income inequality to lower social trust and cohesion, especially in high-income countries. Replicating or updating their analysis for 2010–2020 can confirm or refute the hypothesis within the specified scope.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of the European Social Survey (ESS) trust indicators (2010–2020) for high-income countries with weak welfare states (e.g., US, UK, Southern Europe). — Directly testing the temporal and geographic scope, this source would use repeated measures of social trust and cohesion as dependent variables, with Gini coefficients as the independent variable, controlling for welfare state generosity.

scope.domain: high-income countries with weak welfare states

C006.subject: economic inequality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: economic inequality social mobility]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of income mobility using panel data from the PSID (Panel Study of Income Dynamics) for the US and similar datasets for the UK and Canada, focusing on post-2008 cohorts — This would directly test whether rising inequality after the 2008 crisis correlates with changes in intergenerational or intragenerational social mobility, controlling for policy and economic shocks.

[PATH:theoretical] Comparative policy review of social mobility interventions (e.g., education access, tax credits, union density) across the US, UK, and Canada from 2009-2020 — A theoretical model can assess if inequality stimulates mobility by incentivizing human capital investment or if it instead entrenches advantage, using institutional differences as natural experiments.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on the inequality-mobility relationship in high-income countries, with a focus on post-2008 findings — Synthesizing current evidence can reveal whether the disputed hypothesis holds under different methodological approaches and identify gaps in temporal or geographic coverage.

qualifier.geographic: United States, United Kingdom, and Canada

C007.subject: economic inequality in collectivist societies
C007.object: social cohesion only when inequality is perceived as legitimate or merit-based
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: economic inequality in collectivist societies social cohesion only when inequality is perceived as legitimate or merit-based]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-national survey data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and Asian Barometer on perceived legitimacy of inequality and social trust in Japan, South Korea, and China (post-2000) — Directly tests whether perceived meritocracy moderates the relationship between income inequality and social cohesion in these collectivist societies.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental vignette studies measuring social cohesion responses to inequality scenarios with manipulated legitimacy cues (e.g., merit-based vs. arbitrary inequality) in East Asian samples — Establishes causal evidence for the conditional effect of legitimacy perception on cohesion, controlling for cultural confounds.

scope.domain: collectivist societies with strong meritocratic narratives

qualifier.geographic: East Asian collectivist societies (e.g., Japan, South Korea, China)

C008.subject: economic inequality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: economic inequality social cohesion]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal household panel surveys in East Asia (e.g., China Family Panel Studies, Korean Labor and Income Panel Study) tracking income inequality and social trust indicators since 2000 — Directly tests the temporal and geographic scope by measuring changes in economic inequality and social cohesion over time within collectivist societies.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative cross-national studies of East Asian countries using World Values Survey or Asian Barometer data on social capital and collective action — Provides cross-sectional evidence on whether higher inequality correlates with lower social cohesion in collectivist cultural contexts, controlling for other factors.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of social cohesion in collectivist societies (e.g., work by Markus & Kitayama on cultural interdependence, or Putnam's social capital theory adapted for East Asia) — Helps clarify the mechanisms through which inequality might weaken cohesion in collectivist settings, offering predictions that empirical studies can test.

C011.subject: perceived economic inequality
C011.object: social cohesion only when mediated by reduced trust in institutions
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: perceived economic inequality social cohesion only when mediated by reduced trust in institutions]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative panel data analysis using OECD's Trustlab survey and national inequality metrics (e.g., Gini coefficient) to test mediation via institutional trust over time (2010-2023) — Directly tests the causal mediation pathway by modeling perceived inequality -> institutional trust -> social cohesion, controlling for confounds, across multiple OECD countries.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental vignette studies in representative OECD samples manipulating perceived inequality (e.g., via income gap primes) and measuring trust in institutions and social cohesion intentions — Allows causal identification of the mediation mechanism, isolating perceived inequality's effect on cohesion through trust, overcoming observational data limitations.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing studies on inequality, trust, and social cohesion, focusing on mediation tests and effect sizes in OECD populations (2010-2023) — Synthesizes available evidence to assess consistency of the mediated pathway across contexts, identifying gaps and moderators (e.g., welfare regime, cultural trust baseline).
